paragraphs: Rav Acha Karchana, [Berakhot 33a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.33a.22). Yaakov Karchina, Kiddushin 86a as supplied (compare [Eruvin 86a](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.86a.15)).
In [Shabbat 152a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.152a.5), a certain eunuch said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, “How far is it from here to Karchina?” etc.[^4]

notes.text: The consulted Shabbat paragraph spells out Yehoshua ben Korcha and supports the baldness wordplay. Kiddushin 86a is outside that tractate’s folio range and remains an unresolved printed locator.

The saved whole Davidson Eruvin86a scalar names untitled Yaakov Karchina and his teaching about sinking reeds a handbreadth in water, supporting a matching location alongside supplied Kiddushin86a. The match does not prove the mechanism of the tractate-name discrepancy. The earlier Shabbat152a full-Yehoshua/baldness comparison is inherited, not newly inspected; the source’s own eunuch gloss and distance question remain. No actual place Karchina or common authority for the listed names is established. Full Rav for Ada and Acha is supplied.

The printed notice (vol. III, p. 1037) cites Kiddushin for Yaakov Karchina. The teaching about sinking the ends of reeds a handbreadth is in Eruvin 86a. Sanhedrin 92a and Berakhot 33a give very similar objections about vengeance between divine names, naming Rav Ada and Rav Acha respectively and spelling both epithets Karchina. Rashi on Shabbat 152a explains the distance question as a taunt about Rabbi Yehoshua’s baldness. The parallel wording leaves the listed identities and any actual place identification open.
The parallel challenges in Sanhedrin and Berakhot use Ada and Acha respectively. The Yaakov reading is located at Eruvin 86a. Shabbat uses the similar word in a joke about baldness.
